analysis.one_liner: Bans landlords from using shared pricing algorithms to inflate rents.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 21 House Democrats, never received a hearing or a vote in the House Judiciary Committee and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for landlords with 4 or more rental units to hire pricing-software companies that pool rent and occupancy data from competing landlords and use algorithms to recommend rents. Using such a service would automatically count as an illegal price-fixing agreement under antitrust law. Renters could sue for triple damages, and the FTC, the Justice Department, and state attorneys general could enforce the ban.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters, especially tenants of large corporate landlords whose rents are set or suggested by revenue-management software that pools data across competitors. If rents came down even modestly across the millions of units owned by big landlords, tenants would save money, and the bill would give renters harmed by such pricing a private right to sue for three times their damages plus attorney fees [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Makes it an automatic ("per se") violation of the Sherman Act for a landlord of 4 or more rental units to pay for or subscribe to a pricing service that collects rent, supply, and lease-termination data from competing owners and uses computation to recommend rents, lease terms, or occupancy targets [S2].
Gives any renter harmed by the practice the right to sue in federal court for three times their actual damages plus attorney fees, with possible interest, no matter how small the claim [S2].

Lets a suing renter strike down pre-dispute arbitration clauses and class-action waivers tied to a violation, so tenants could join together in court instead of being forced into individual arbitration [S2].

Lowers the pleading bar for renters: a complaint only has to plausibly allege that landlords coordinated pricing in parallel and need not rule out that each landlord acted independently, addressing how hard secret algorithmic price-fixing is to prove [S2].

Gives the FTC, the Attorney General, and every state attorney general power to enforce the ban, lets the FTC sue directly for civil penalties, and preserves any stronger state, tribal, or city laws on the same subject [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Rental pricing and revenue-management software companies (the business model of pooling competitor data to recommend rents would be a per se antitrust violation) and the large landlords that subscribe to them, who would face automatic legal liability, private lawsuits with triple damages, and the need to exit those services. Some of those costs could be passed through to renters through compliance and litigation expenses [S2].

drawbacks.text: The bill sweeps broadly: "coordinator" includes a landlord running pricing analytics for its own units, and the ban applies to owners of just 4 units, so small landlords who use common off-the-shelf software could face automatic antitrust liability and lawsuit risk, not just RealPage-style networks [S2].

The relaxed pleading standard — where "consciously parallel pricing coordination" alone plausibly pleads a conspiracy — and the per se rule raise litigation exposure sharply, and an honest supporter would acknowledge that some cases would target landlords who set prices independently using the same market data [S2].

Defenders of revenue-management software argue it simply gives small landlords the up-to-the-minute market data that large chains already gather themselves, so banning shared tools could entrench the information advantage of the biggest landlords rather than lower rents [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For renters, the upside is real: pricing algorithms that pool data across competing landlords are exactly the kind of coordination antitrust law was built for, and the bill adds treble-damage private suits, class-action rights, and multi-agency enforcement [S2]. The costs are a deliberately aggressive design — a per se rule, a low pleading bar, and coverage down to 4-unit owners — that would sweep in some small landlords and independent price-setters and generate heavy litigation. A narrower bill limited to coordinators who pool data across unrelated owners would have captured most of the benefit with less collateral exposure.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Becca Balint introduced the bill on June 5, 2024, joined by eight original cosponsors, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S4].
Twenty-one House members cosponsored the bill; every one of them was a Democrat [S3].

The action history shows no hearing, no committee markup, and no floor vote after the referral — the bill sat in committee for the remaining seven months of the 118th Congress and expired on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Rental pricing software companies and the large landlords that subscribe to them are better off, because the per se ban and renters' private right to action never advanced. Renters are no worse off in law but gained nothing from Congress either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Rental software firms and big landlords

for.name: Rep. Becca Balint
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 21 cosponsors, all Democrats

for.name: 21 House Democrats, including Reps. Nadler, Jayapal, Norton, Gomez, and Omar
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; several were original cosponsors named at introduction

against.name: Rep. Jim Jordan
against.role: Chair, House Committee on the Judiciary
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress

against.name: RealPage and the revenue-management software industry
against.role: Pricing software vendor for large landlords
against.what_they_did: The bill targeted its business model directly; the company faced a Justice Department antitrust suit over the same pricing software in 2024 and lobbied against similar bans at the state and local level

against.name: Large corporate landlords and apartment industry groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on revenue-management tools that the industry credits with raising occupancy and rents

sides.party_line_note: All 21 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on; with Republicans controlling the House and the Judiciary Committee, the bill never advanced [S3].

industries.industry: Rental pricing and revenue-management software (e.g., RealPage-style coordinators)
industries.note: The bill makes the industry's core product — pooling rent, supply, and lease-expiration data from competing landlords and using algorithms to recommend rents — an automatic antitrust violation, with the FTC, the Justice Department, state attorneys general, and private renters all able to sue. Its business model would be illegal rather than merely regulated [S2].

industries.industry: Large corporate landlords and property managers
industries.note: Subscribing to a coordinating service would itself be a per se Sherman Act violation, exposing owners of 4 or more units to government enforcement and renter lawsuits with triple damages, so big landlords would have to drop these tools or face liability [S2].
